The upcoming MacBook Ultra is never going to be cheap. Besides a brand-new, slimmer design, an OLED display, and touch functionality, there's also the price hike driven by rising memory costs to consider. The latest reports suggest that manufacturing costs could be pushed even higher.

Apple has always liked to introduce multiple suppliers for components to improve display supply stability and secure the best pricing. It had originally hoped to follow this approach with the MacBook Ultra as well. However, according to supply chain sources, Apple has decided to use only a single display supplier...

Apple has three display partners across different product lines: Samsung, LG, and BOE (京東方). BOE currently only produces screens for the company's lower-end products, while high-end display orders are shared between Samsung and LG.

The MacBook Ultra will feature the most sophisticated display ever on an Apple product. Combining two-stack tandem OLED technology with touch functionality on the larger sizes required for a laptop is no easy feat. The latest supply chain report indicates that Apple has decided to exclusively source the relevant panels from Samsung.

According to The Elec, LG failed to meet Apple's required production volume.

Apple demanded the use of large substrates for mass production. Samsung Display responded with its 8.6-generation OLED production line, while LG Display was reportedly considering sticking with its existing 6-generation production line. Although it is still feasible to produce laptop OLED panels on a 6-generation line, substrate efficiency and output are lower than on an 8.6-generation line. Since initial product output may be too low, Apple has therefore chosen Samsung Display as its sole supplier.

It seems LG's production capacity is too small, and the logistical complexity of dual sourcing isn't worth it. LG is not expected to produce displays for this flagship MacBook before 2029.

This clearly puts Samsung in a stronger position in panel price negotiations, which is expected to drive up Apple's manufacturing costs. Apple will very likely pass this expense on to consumers, just as it has handled the rise in memory costs.

Given that the MacBook Ultra's price may be staggeringly high, how likely are you to consider upgrading? Feel free to share your thoughts in the comments section.
